entries.source_text: This study examines changes in long-distance relationships between grandparents and their adolescent grandchildren by identifying relational turning points and trajectories. Qualitative analysis of data collected from interviews with grandparents yielded 100 unique turning points. Constant comparative analysis revealed eight distinct categories of relational turning points; Spending Time Together, Family Relational Dynamics, Geographic Distance, Lack of Relational Investment, Use of Technology, Relational Investment, Lack of Free Time, and Grandchild Gaining Independence. These varied in the degree to which they positively or negatively impacted relational closeness. Application of the Retrospective Interview Technique (RIT) yielded five distinctive relational trajectories: Decrease in Closeness, Increase in Closeness, Multidimensional Changes in Closeness, Minimal Changes in Closeness, and Consistent Relational Closeness. The results expose the communicative challenges faced by long-distance-grandparents, the diversity of these relationships, and the ways in which grandparenting bonds change over time. Implications for an enriched understanding of grandparenting relationships and practical applications for families are explored.

entries.source_text: Quality grandparenting relationships can be a source of stability, social support, and satisfaction in families. Children, their parents, and grandparents themselves are likely to benefit when these relationships are maintained over time. Moreover, support provided by grandparents may reduce a family's need for resources that might otherwise be provided by the state, such as subsidized daycare, after-school programs, or respite services for families in crisis (Dolbin-McNab & Keiley, 2009). Although grandparenting was neglected by family scholars for many years, interest has surged in the last decade, due in part to persuasive calls for new and better research on grandparent–grandchild relationships (Harwood, 2000a; Soliz, Lin, Anderson, & Harwood, 2006). The current study builds on previous research on the factors that contribute to stability and change in these relationships (Holladay et al., 1998). We focus on the grandchild's adolescence, a potentially tumultuous developmental period in which grandparents can be an important source of support (Attar-Schwartz, Tan, & Buchanan, 2009). Researchers have noted (e.g., Holladay & Seipke, 2007) that grandparents face relational challenges when they are geographically-separated from family, but studies suggest that many of them find ways to sustain emotionally close bonds with distant grandchildren (Waldron, Giteson, & Kelley, 2005). Our study qualitatively analyzes the relational practices and life events that increase or decrease the quality of long distance grandparenting relationships over the course of adolescence.

entries.source_text: Although grandparenting relationships are common, they vary considerably. This variability became evident in early work by Neugarten and Weinstein (1964), who observed a variety of grandparenting styles. For example, some grandparents were counted on as sources of advice and wisdom. Others primarily served as fun-seeking companions. Some were highly engaged in family maintenance, sometimes serving as surrogate parents. A fourth group, by preference or due to circumstances, remained distant and uninvolved. Later empirical research examined the ways in which grandparents performed their roles, including those who were influential, supportive, passive, authority-oriented, and detached (Mueller, Wilhelm, & Elder, 2002). More recently, Soliz (2008) identified kinds of “support enactments” that grandparents contribute including emotional support, stability, peacekeeping, “straight talking”, and information about family history.

entries.source_text: These role performances may change over time as the grandparent adjusts to the needs of the developing grandchild and the changing realities of family life. During the early years, grandchildren may benefit from the presence and physical affection of grandparents (Holladay & Seipke, 2007). This may change as the child enters adolescence; time spent with grandparents may diminish as school commitments and peer relationships become more consuming. It appears that frequency of communication, parental encouragement, and grandparents' efforts to remain involved may offset the tendency of adolescents to become more emotionally distant (Attar-Schwartz et al., 2009). Life events may be a catalyst for increased closeness, as when the adolescent's parents experience a stressful divorce (Soliz, 2008). As the grandchild enters late adolescence/young adulthood, the relationship may change again; grandchildren may be less emotionally close to their grandparents, but they often report high levels of appreciation and respect (Attar-Schwartz et al., 2009).

entries.source_text: Long distance grandparenting is another variation of this traditional family role (Harwood, 2000b). Geographic separation from grandchildren is fairly common in middle class U.S. families, due to job-related relocation, children leaving home for college, and the mobility of grandparents who relocate after retiring from the workforce (Waldron, Giteson, & Kelley, 2005; Waldron, Giteson, Kelley, & Regalado, 2005). Reviews of this literature suggest that geographic proximity fosters emotional closeness in grandparenting relationships (Harwood, 2007). In a study of long distance grandparents living in a Florida retirement community, Holladay and Seipke (2007) found that most respondents experienced face-to-face communication with grandchildren just “a few times” each year or less. Waldron and colleagues found that maintaining relationships with distant grandchildren was a source of concern for grandparents living in Arizona retirement communities. However, those who used electronic communication to stay in touch with grandchildren reported higher levels of life satisfaction. Other studies found that closeness in long distance relationships can be sustained through frequent email or phone conversations, particularly if communication is initiated by the grandchild (Harwood, 2000a; Holladay & Seipke, 2007).

entries.source_text: Taken as a whole, the literature suggests that long distance grandparenting relationships are often experienced as challenging, and they require grandparents to invest considerable effort in relationship-maintenance (Waldron & Waldron, 2009). Few researchers have consulted with grandparents to understand their perspectives on factors that spur positive or negative changes in long distance grandparenting relationships.

entries.source_text: A turning point is a transformative event in which a relationship is changed in some way (Baxter & Erbert, 1999). The turning point framework focuses attention on increases and decreases in feelings of psychological closeness, making it possible to trace relational trajectories over long periods of the life course (Cappeliez, Beaupré, & Robitaille, 2008). Several existing studies have explored turning points involving grandparents. Dun (2010) studied the period around the birth of a new grandchild by 23 parents. Distance was a factor when grandparents lived too far away to be helpful to the parent or personally involved with the grandchild. Other changes stemmed from the larger ecological field of family life. Dun's study of turning points is instructive but limited by its focus on the earliest months of the grandchild's life, when the grandparenting relationship has yet to mature.

entries.source_text: More applicable is a qualitative study of turning points in relationships between grandmothers and granddaughters by Holladay et al. (1998). Based on interviews with 42 young adult females (mean age = 19 years), researchers concluded that relational closeness increased due to shared activities, serious health events among family members, and family disruptions. An increase in geographic proximity was also associated with increased closeness. Negative relational encounters with the grandmother were associated with decreased closeness, as were geographic separations and the grandchild leaving home to attend college. Related work (e.g., Holladay & Seipke, 2007; Mansson, 2013; Mansson & Booth Butterfield, 2011) fails to consider relational changes that occur in response to life events or maturation. Instead, patterns of communication measured at one point in time are conceptualized as stable indicators of relational quality and assumed to persist over time.

entries.source_text: Grandparent–grandchild relationships are likely to change, particularly as a grandchild moves through adolescence. However, we know little about the trajectories of these relationships as they are experienced by grandparents. Do they consistently decrease in closeness, as some researchers have speculated (e.g. Attar-Schwartz et al., 2009) due to the grandchildren becoming invested in their peer groups and school commitments? It may be that some relationships actually become closer over time and others cycle between states of closeness and distance in response to life events (Holladay et al., 1998). Thus, we anticipated that grandparents would report varying trajectories of relational closeness and that these trajectories would be contingent on life events of both the grandchild and grandparent as well as events within the family. At the same time, the exact nature of these trajectories could not be predicted, so we posed Research Question 1 to guide our analysis.

entries.source_text: Holladay et al. (1998) found that geographic separation from a grandmother identified as a negative turning point for granddaughters. These findings encouraged us to examine turning points in long distance relationships exclusively. Grandparents shoulder much responsibility for maintaining the emotional vitality of these bonds; they presumably develop unique relational insights about the family dynamics that shape the relationship. Yet, researchers have yet to study turning points from a grandparent's perspective. Our second research question focused on identifying the specific turning points that shape these relational trajectories. Based on past research, we certainly anticipated geographic distance to play a unique role in the relational events reported by grandparents and suspected that grandparents who positively adapt to the geographic distance may maintain higher levels of relational quality with their grandchildren over time. However, given that other possibilities were likely to surface, our efforts were guided by this research question.

entries.source_text: Participants were recruited through collaboration with the Osher Lifelong Learning Institute, a noncredit university-sponsored educational program designed for older members of the local community. All current participants of the Osher Lifelong Learning Institute at Arizona State University were sent an email or provided handouts describing the study and eligibility for participation. Eligibility for participation required participants to have at least one grandchild between the ages of 12 and 19 and to agree with the following statement, adapted from Guldner and Swensen (1995): “At least one of my grandchildren lives far enough away from me that it would be very difficult or impossible to see them every day”.

entries.source_text: Qualitative, semi-structured interviews were conducted with thirty-five (N = 35) participants in their homes and on the campus of a large university. Five interviews could not be transcribed. The ages of participants ranged from 60 to 82 years (M = 70.9, SD = 5.34) while the ages of the grandchildren ranged between 12 and 19 (M = 14.7, SD = 2.36). Twenty-nine participants identified their race/ethnicity as Caucasian, one participant was identified as Hispanic. All participants lived independent of professional caregivers; twenty-three participants lived either part time or full time in a residential retirement community while seven participants lived in homes outside of retirement communities. Twenty-one participants were female (N = 21), and nine participants were male (N = 9). Twenty-six participants were married and four participants were identified as single/widowed/divorced. Our previous studies of this population indicated that questions about income tended to make participants uncomfortable, so we refrained from asking. However, the larger population OSHER life-long learning students were consistently identified as having a “mid-range” income, and homes in the retirement community sell for prices near or slightly above the national average. Most residents have completed at least some college and roughly 50% have college degrees. Thus, our sample consists primarily of middle class, married, fairly-well educated retired persons.

entries.source_text: Turning points were generated using the Retrospective Interview Technique (RIT), in which informants are interviewed about turning points that have taken place within the relationship. Participants were then asked to graph those turning points on a grid in order to generate an understanding of how the relationship has changed over time and what events caused these changes (Baxter & Pittman, 2001). RIT is a particularly interactive methodology that allows the participant and the researcher to gain a visual representation of the relationship and is especially suitable for building participant/researcher rapport. Thus, this strategy is appropriate for gaining a valid understanding of relational events that shape the closeness of grandparents and their grandchildren and allows these events to be understood from a developmental perspective.

entries.source_text: The term ‘closeness’ was isolated and discussed at great length in order to ensure that participants understood this important aspect of the study. Consistent with Golish (2000), closeness was defined as the psychological bond that a grandparent feels towards the grandchild. Once it was evident that participants understood the definition of relational closeness, the interview shifted to discuss and define turning points that cause changes in relational closeness. The theoretical concept of relational turning points was thoroughly discussed and participants were given several examples of turning points cited from previous research studies (e.g. Holladay et al., 1998) such as a death in the family, marriage, moving out of state, or the birth of a child. Defining these terms early in the interview process ensured that participants were able to think about these relationships in ways that correlate to the purpose of the research study.

entries.source_text: Next, participants were asked to select one of their long-distance grandchildren to discuss during the interview. They were then presented with a RIT graph that included the level of closeness on the y-axis (1 — most close; 5 — least close) and the age of the child on the x-axis. Participants plotted changes in relational closeness beginning at age five until the grandchild's current age. Beginning the study of relational closeness at age five was justified not only by similar retrospective research, (Golish, 2000) but also by Piaget's theory of the preoperational stage of cognitive development. At the preoperational stage, which occurs around age five, a child produces mental abilities that are essential to relational development (Miller & Church, 2003). The interview then transitioned to a discussion of each turning point. Interviews ranged from approximately 7 min to 45 min in length. Immediately following the interview, a transcript was made from the recording, yielding 116 pages of double-spaced text. The thirty hand-drawn RIT graphs were converted to digital displays (see Figs. 1–5).

entries.source_text: The constant comparative method (Glaser & Strauss, 1967) utilizes comparing and contrasting as the main intellectual tools for establishing boundaries of categories and discerning conceptual similarities between categories (Tesch, 1990). We utilized constant comparative method to identify a typology of turning points and relational trajectories identified by participants. Each turning point was compared with the previous turning points in an effort to identify its similarities and differences. Coding notes documented the reasons for grouping and separating turning point descriptions. The process was guided both by our understanding of turning points reported by earlier authors and also by our expectation that long distance relationships may be subjected to unique forces of change. An initial set of categories was created by the first author based on a review of a sample of the interviews. In an effort to enhance the representativeness and clarity of the categories, their definitions and examples were discussed with the second author and with several grandparents. This process resulted in refined definitions for several categories and the collapsing of several categories deemed to be similar in meaning. The first author then reapplied the category system to the whole data set as she looked closely for negative cases. None were found. Theoretical saturation appeared to be reached after roughly 75% of the data were examined, but the whole data set was coded.

entries.source_text: Fig. 1 displays trajectories that feature marked decreases in relational closeness over time. Participants tended to describe a period of early closeness with their grandchild then a subtle or dramatic decline in closeness, indicating that the trajectories change at different rates. It appears that most of these relationships began with relatively high levels of closeness and that many began to wane in closeness at similar points in grandchild development. A second type of trajectory (Fig. 2) is characterized by consistency and stability. These participants drew a straight line on the RIT graph, indicating that they had not experienced any changes in relational closeness. The lines were drawn at different points on the graph, indicating that some grandparents maintained significant closeness while others experienced consistently distant relationships (5 on the Likert-type scale).

entries.source_text: The results of this study contribute to the growing literature on long distance grandparenting relationships. They do so by identifying several distinct change trajectories reported by grandparents as well as positive and negative turning points in their relationships with adolescent grandchildren. As have other researchers (e.g., Holladay et al., 1998) we found the turning points methodology to be useful in generating qualitative data regarding changes in relational closeness. The reports of just 22 participants yielded more than 100 substantive change events—a rich set of insights about the circumstances that help and hinder grandparenting bonds. At the same time, eight grandparents perceived no changes in closeness, indicating that the turning point assumptions may not apply universally, a point explored recently by other researchers (Corman, Noonan, Reichman, & Schwartz-Soicher, 2011). These results imply that factors contributing to both stability and change should be examined in studies of this type.

entries.source_text: Our analysis of relational trajectories suggested more variety in relational paths than might be expected from previous literature. About one-third of the long distance grandparents observed a marked decline as the grandchild developed into adolescence. This decline has been attributed to the child's growing independence and engagement with an expanding social network of peers and adults (Harwood, 2007). Our results indicate that the growing social networks and activity demands on adolescents make it more difficult (and perhaps reduce the motivation) to invest effort in maintaining the relationship. Identity affirmation and other relational rewards previously conveyed by the grandparent may now be available from other sources. At the same time, our participants reported life changes such as retirement or illness during this period. Consistent with previous work (Holladay et al., 1998), grandparents in our study reported moving away during the adolescent years or reported their own engagements in new activities. In this way, the trend toward declining closeness appears to be exacerbated by life changes of both parties.

entries.source_text: Our data failed to support the idea that relational closeness inevitably declines over time. Indeed, interviewees often reported stability, even during the grandchild's adolescence. Some grandparents simply perceived no change over time. In at least one case, low relational closeness reflected the grandparent's limited involvement in family life from the grandchild's earliest years. But other grandparents seemed to cultivate stability through an intentional effort to engage with the adolescent child. They did so by scheduling visits or adopting new forms of communication, such as texting, social media, or Skype. This finding is consistent with that of Holladay and Seipke (2007) who suggested that grandparents remain relatively satisfied with long distance relationships, in part by substituting telephone conversations for personal contacts with the grandchild. Our data suggest that continued relational investment by either party, or the lack thereof, is perceived as a relational turning point.

entries.source_text: When closeness ebbed during adolescence, grandparents reported making adjustments, such as planning a visit or initiating contact through social media. Apparently, long-distance bonds, similar to face-to-face relationships (see Mansson, Myers, & Turner, 2010), can be steadied when the parties engage actively in relationship maintenance practices. This finding may be particularly heartening for grandparents who wonder how the relationship might be sustained through the potentially challenging adolescent period. It is worth noting, however, that a small but notable portion of these relationships experienced more dramatic changes. As observed by others, (e.g., Holladay et al., 1998) these changes were sometimes attributable to major disruptions in family life, such as death, illness or divorce of the parents.

entries.source_text: Taken together, the results pertaining to RQ1 tell us that long distance grandparents might expect some decline in the closeness of their relationships with adolescent grandchildren. However, they also suggest that geographic distance is not the relational barrier it appeared to be at an earlier time (e.g., Harwood, 2000a). The last decade has seen a surge in the use of cell phones and social media platforms, particularly by adolescents. In some ways, technology has created opportunities for grandparents to communicate directly with grandchildren and to stay abreast of their lives. In our interviews, it appeared that grandparents who make use of these technologies are more likely to sustain close relationships over time.

entries.source_text: Family Relational Dynamics was a complicated theme, including instances of parental divorce, changes in living arrangements, abuse, and other shifts in the ecology of the family system. Previously Soliz (2008) argued that grandparents can be important sources of support to adolescents during divorce. Our own results are less encouraging, or at least ambivalent in this regard. In some cases, such as an instance when a grandmother shared living space with the grandchild and recently divorced mother, the opportunities for new companionship and routine conversation were viewed as a positive turning point. entries.source_text: A unanimously negative turning point category, Lack of Relational Investment, displayed a general feeling of disinterest in the relationship from either the grandparent or the grandchild. Within this category, participants often characterized the relationship as “one sided”, indicating that their efforts to communicate through letters, phone calls, or inviting their grandchild to visit are not reciprocated by their adolescent grandchildren. The symbolic importance of reciprocation to grandparents has been noted elsewhere (Harwood, 2000; Holladay & Seipke, 2007). It seems that these experiences left participants feeling psychologically “shut out” by their grandchildren and in some cases undermined their desire to invest in the relationship. Although also a negative turning point, Lack of Free Time was generalized as less detrimental to the relationship. A grandchild having limited time to spend with a grandparent was often seen as a necessary component of child development which participants generally did not take personally. The impact on closeness, although negative, was not as substantial. This is perhaps because participants were more accepting of a grandchild's inability to make significant relational investments as a result of being involved in many activities.

entries.source_text: Our results update earlier work, completed before the rapid emergence of social media (e.g., Harwood, 2000b). Use of Technology was cited as a positive turning point by grandparents. The adoption of Skype, Facebook, and text messaging was perceived to increase closeness. Indeed, several participants claimed technology to facilitate other closeness enhancing experiences and conversations. Participants credited technology for making communication more frequent and versatile; grandparents who use Facebook spoke of the joy of seeing recent photographs or posts and claimed to feel more involved in their grandchild's life as a result. For some, Facebook expanded their relational role, allowing them to participate in the adolescent's network of peers and to share in interactions (such as status posting) that were previously unknown or off limits. In this way, technology may be particularly helpful during the adolescent years when peer influence expands, sometimes to the exclusion of the grandparenting relationship. Previous work (Mansson, 2013) indicates that college-aged grandchildren respond positively when grandparents celebrate their achievements, share humor, and contribute positive memories. Social media offer long distance grandparents platforms for just these kinds of communication.

entries.source_text: The category, Grandchild Gaining Independence, was an expected theme due to our concern with grandchildren ages 12–19. Participants spoke of grandchildren becoming teenagers and preferring to spend time with friends during this developmental stage. Participants spoke of raising their own children and remembered the teenage years as a phase—one which they attributed to unpredictable shifts in hormones. entries.source_text: Results of this study must be interpreted with some caution. One limitation stems from the highly subjective nature of relational closeness. Although a key component of the turning point methodology involved clarification of the term “closeness”, grandparents may apply the term differently. Some long distance grandparents seemed to have been quite uninvolved (by choice or circumstance) in their grandchildren's lives from the very beginning; a result is that they perceived no turning points. Another limitation involves the sample, which is limited in cultural diversity. Future research should examine long distance grandparenting in cultural contexts, such as the traditional Hispanic family, where geographic separation is likely to be unsettling, stigmatized, and challenging. Finally, the relational trajectories reported here are partial. Some of the grandchildren had yet to complete adolescence. We did not track turning points before the age of five. Thus we may have missed some of the early or later life events that shape the closeness of relationships of this type.

entries.source_text: Several avenues of additional research present themselves. First, the use of emerging technology in long-distance grandparenting relationships is a rich area of inquiry. The extent to which relationships can be enhanced by photo-sharing, Skype, and other tools has yet to be fully explored. Another concern is the role of relational expectancies. It appeared that negative turning points were often the result of unfulfilled expectations about spending time with a grandchild. It may be that expectancy match is more important than any particular relational practice. Finally, cultural differences in long distance grandparenting need to be understood. How do expectations and communication practices vary across ethnic groups, particularly when cultural norms support strong social ties among extended family members, including adolescents and their grandparents?

entries.source_text: Our results have practical implications for grandparents and those who work with them. First, grandparents may be able to increase or stabilize closeness in some relationships. Finding ways to spend time with distant grandchildren (e.g. scheduling visits or sharing a vacation) is one of those. Learning to use emerging technology is another positive step, one that might be particularly important for grandparents living at a distance. Memories can be sources of strength. Grandparents who recalled the adolescent years of their own children seemed better able to weather the changes of adolescent grandchildren. Changed expectations may be helpful as the grandchild ages; grandparents who tempered their expectations about the adolescent's investment of time and effort seemed to experience less disappointment. Finally, the largely negative impact of disruption of the family system should be of interest to those who counsel families. Contrary to some prior research, the grandparent and grandchild tended not to draw closer during family crises, perhaps due to the complications of distance. Finding ways to keep these grandparents involved and supportive of adolescents during times of family distress might be a point of discussion during family therapy.
